listening.title: Registering for a bookshop volunteer shift
listening.script:
Organiser: Hello, Page Turners charity bookshop.
Caller: Hello. I saw your notice asking for volunteers. I’ve recently moved to the area and have some free time each week. I’ve worked in a shop before, though not with books. Are you still looking for people?
Organiser: We are, especially for regular shifts. We don’t expect volunteers to know every author. Being willing to ask questions and follow the stock procedure matters more. Could I take your name?
Caller: It’s Nadia Seldon. S-E-L-D-O-N. People sometimes write Sheldon, but there’s no H. I live close enough to walk, so I wouldn’t depend on the bus for an early start.
Organiser: Thank you. Which days could you offer? We have a full team on Saturday at present, but weekday afternoons are more difficult to cover.
Caller: My first thought was Wednesday, but I’ve enrolled on a Wednesday course. I can do Monday every week. I’d rather promise one reliable day than offer several and keep changing them.
Organiser: That would be excellent. The afternoon shift begins at one, but for your first visit please come at twelve thirty. The supervisor can show you the building before customers arrive for the afternoon session.
Caller: All right, 12:30 on Monday. Is it a long shift?
Organiser: Three hours normally. For the induction we’ll keep it to two if you prefer, though it’s useful to see the closing routine on a later visit. You can discuss that with the supervisor when you know your other commitments.
Caller: What kind of work needs doing? I’m happy speaking to customers, but I wouldn’t want to start on the till without training.
Organiser: You won’t. New volunteers usually begin with sorting. Donations come in mixed boxes, and we separate saleable books from items needing specialist advice. You’ll work with an experienced person rather than decide alone what an unfamiliar volume is worth.
Caller: That sounds interesting. Should I bring any documents for the registration?
Organiser: Bring one reference, please, from somebody outside your household. A former work supervisor is fine. We don’t need your school certificates or a formal essay about why you like reading.
---
Caller: Could you explain where to arrive? I know the shop front, but I imagine you don’t want me knocking while it’s closed.
Organiser: Use the rear door on your first day. It’s reached from the small lane beside the café. The front shutters will still be down at twelve thirty, and the bell there isn’t easy to hear from the stockroom.
Caller: I’ll find it. What should I wear? The notice mentioned comfortable shoes.
Organiser: Yes, and ordinary clothes you don’t mind getting dusty. We’ll provide a badge once you’ve registered. Please wear it on the shop floor so customers can tell who is working. There’s no uniform purchase.
Caller: Are volunteers expected to move heavy boxes? I can carry a few books but should avoid lifting something large from the floor.
Organiser: We have a trolley, and heavy boxes should be split into smaller loads. Tell the supervisor about any task you shouldn’t do. Nobody is expected to prove enthusiasm by taking a risk, and there’s plenty of work that doesn’t involve lifting.
Caller: Good. I assume personal belongings stay somewhere away from donations?
Organiser: There are lockers in the office. Please don’t leave a bag on the sorting table, because it could be mistaken for something brought in by a donor. Bring a small padlock if you’d like to lock your locker.
Caller: I have one at home. What if I can’t make a shift after I’ve joined?
Organiser: Call the supervisor as early as possible. Text is fine if the shop is closed, but please don’t just put a message in the social-media group. It can get buried under photographs and general conversation. A direct message lets us arrange cover.
Caller: Understood. I’ll get the reference organised and see you on Monday.
Organiser: I’ll email the induction outline today. Read it before you come if you can, but don’t worry about memorising the stock categories. The first visit is for learning the system, not passing a test.

listening.title: Tour of the Westfield recreation centre
listening.script:
Guide: Welcome to Westfield. I’ll explain the rooms using the plan on your information sheet, then mention changes to our membership arrangements. You are standing at reception, shown at the bottom of the plan. The corridor runs straight towards the outdoor court at the top. Left and right refer to the direction you’re facing now, not to somebody returning from the court. The central corridor stays clear; equipment should never be left there, even for a minute between classes.
The room immediately to your right is the equipment store. It has double doors, so returning larger items is easier. Members can borrow rackets there, but staff need to record the number before you take them outside. Please don’t help yourself just because another customer has left the door open. Opposite, immediately to your left, is a staff room that is not open to members.
Walk towards the court and you’ll reach two more rooms. The first on the left is the exercise studio. This is where stretching and low-impact classes take place. There are mirrors along one wall, but don’t confuse it with the dance studio at our other building. Across the corridor, the first room on the right beyond the store is the changing area. There are accessible facilities within it, so you don’t need to ask for a separate key at reception.
Continue to the last pair of rooms. On the left, just before the door to the court, is the first-aid room. It is staffed during all organised sessions. On the right is the meeting room, where club organisers can discuss events without standing in reception. That room used to contain vending machines. We’ve moved refreshments into the entrance area to free it for meetings and small training sessions.
---
Outdoor-court bookings are now released seven days ahead. Previously, some members reserved several weeks in advance and then cancelled shortly before playing, leaving little opportunity for others. The shorter window is intended to improve access. It isn’t a response to resurfacing work; that was finished last month and doesn’t affect the current schedule.
Equipment hire is included in the membership price for ordinary sessions. However, lost items must still be paid for. We don’t want members to avoid trying a new sport because they haven’t bought the right racket, but borrowing carries responsibility. If you find a defect before playing, show staff so that it isn’t attributed to you when you return the item.
Our introductory classes have a new attendance rule. You may reserve a place without paying an extra class fee, but if you cannot come, cancel by the previous evening. Two unexplained absences in a month lead to a temporary booking restriction. The aim is to release unused places, not collect penalties from people whose circumstances change unexpectedly.
Children under twelve must be accompanied in the building, except when handed over to a registered children’s class. An adult waiting in the café has not automatically completed that handover. Please speak to the class leader, who keeps a register. If you are collecting for another family, make sure the arrangement has been recorded before the session ends.
Finally, we are looking for feedback on quieter opening periods. We already know that Saturday morning is busy. What we need now is information from people who would use the centre at other times if a particular activity were offered. The short form asks about feasible times as well as preferred activities. A popular suggestion isn’t useful if everyone who chooses it is unavailable when the room can actually be staffed.

listening.title: Testing a model bridge
listening.script:
Tutor: Your bridge project report is due next week. How did the first test go?
Nora: The model carried more weight than we expected, but it failed suddenly. We thought the main beam would bend first. Instead, a connection near the support pulled apart.
Ethan: We used the right dimensions from the drawing, so at first we blamed the material. Looking again at the video, we saw the connection moving before the beam changed shape.
Tutor: That’s an important observation. A structure is not stronger than every point through which the load must pass. Did you record where each weight was placed?
Nora: Yes, but our first diagram wasn’t precise enough. The weights were spread over a wider area in one test. We need a loading template so that the comparison isn’t affected by where we happen to set them down.
Ethan: We also want to repeat the test on more than one model. Otherwise one badly made connection could be mistaken for the inevitable behaviour of the design.
Tutor: Sensible. Keep construction records so you can discuss differences. Don’t quietly discard a model because it performs less well than you hoped. A poor result may be telling you something about how difficult the design is to build consistently.
Nora: We considered changing the material and the joint together, but then we’d be unable to tell which change mattered.
Ethan: So we’ll first change only the joint, keeping the other dimensions and material the same. If that improves performance, we’ll still need to say how many tests support the claim.
Tutor: Good. What will you count as failure? Total collapse is easy to identify, but a real bridge can become unusable before that.
Nora: We can measure deflection at the centre and set a limit before testing. The report will distinguish exceeding that limit from final collapse.
Tutor: Exactly. A stated criterion makes the comparison meaningful. It also prevents you from redefining success after seeing which version looks best.
---
Ethan: For the next test, we need some equipment. The scale is available in our lab, but the displacement sensor requires booking from the engineering store. We should reserve that today rather than assume it will be there.
Nora: I can arrange the sensor. What about the loading template?
Ethan: That’s the piece we should try out before the main test. The current cardboard version slides when we add weights. If it changes position, the careful markings won’t help us.
Tutor: Make a pilot version and check the practical handling. A procedure can look rigorous on paper and still be impossible to carry out consistently with the hands and space available.
Nora: The safety screen has already been checked by the technician. We have written confirmation, so that item is complete.
Tutor: Keep the confirmation with the risk assessment. Nobody should stand in line with a joint that might release a fragment.
Ethan: Our draft introduction includes a long history of famous bridges. It takes up most of the word allowance without explaining our experiment. We’ll remove that section and use the space for the joint design and testing procedure.
Tutor: A brief context is enough. The reader needs to understand your question, not prove that you have looked at many photographs.
Nora: Finally, the cost comparison. We can’t finish it until we know how much extra material the revised joint uses. We’ll calculate that after constructing the final models.
Ethan: And include labour time separately. A joint that uses very little material but takes much longer to make might not be the better option in every setting.
Tutor: Excellent. Just keep the scope clear. A classroom model can demonstrate a principle and expose construction issues. It cannot certify the safety of a full-size bridge. Your conclusions should be ambitious enough to answer your question and restrained enough to respect that difference.

listening.title: Designing a household waste audit
listening.script:
Lecturer: A town trying to reduce household waste needs to know more than the weight arriving at a disposal site. It needs an account of what is discarded, where it comes from and which changes could realistically prevent it. Today we’ll follow the design of a fictional waste audit. The first step is to define the boundary. Does the study cover homes only, or also restaurants and offices? If these sources are mixed without a record, a large quantity of food waste might be wrongly attributed to households when businesses produced much of it.
The team then defines the period. A holiday week may differ from an ordinary working week, and one season may not represent the year. Repeating observations can reveal variation, but the budget rarely permits continuous measurement everywhere. Researchers therefore choose sampling dates deliberately and state what they cannot represent. They should avoid selecting only the easiest collection days. A timetable is part of the method, not an administrative detail that can be changed casually once inconvenient conditions appear.
Recruitment matters too. Volunteers who are especially interested in reducing waste may already behave differently from other households. A study based entirely on those volunteers could underestimate ordinary discarding. The fictional team selects addresses from a defined list and makes several attempts to invite each selected household. Participation remains optional, and non-response is recorded. Researchers cannot compel people to share private details. They can, however, describe how the eventual sample differs from the population they hoped to study rather than silently calling it representative.
Before weighing begins, the team establishes categories. Too few categories hide useful distinctions; too many make sorting slow and unreliable. Food that might have been eaten is separated from unavoidable remains within the study’s stated definition. Packaging is classified by material where this can be done consistently. Staff practise on a pilot sample and discuss ambiguous items. A written guide records decisions so that two sorters do not place the same object in different categories simply because each has a different intuition about where it belongs.
Containers have weight of their own. Scales are checked, and the weight of an empty container is recorded so it can be subtracted from the total. Otherwise a heavy collection box could look like a household producing more rubbish. Wet conditions create another complication: absorbed water can alter measured mass. The team records relevant conditions and uses a consistent handling procedure. Apparent numerical precision is not a substitute for knowing what entered the weighing process. A balance showing many decimal places cannot correct a badly defined measurement.
Privacy requires practical arrangements throughout. Bags may contain names, addresses or information about household routines. Staff receive training, identifiable material is not photographed for publicity, and records use codes rather than residents' names. The public report describes groups, not a league table of individual homes. The purpose is to improve a service and identify preventable waste, not embarrass participants into a particular performance. If people fear exposure, they may change what they put out or decline to take part, damaging both trust and the evidence.
Analysis compares like with like where possible. Total weight alone can be misleading when household sizes differ, so the team records the number of residents and considers an appropriate rate. Yet one rate cannot explain every difference: a household may have visitors, work away or use another disposal route. Interviews can add context but also introduce recall errors. The report keeps direct measurements distinct from explanations offered afterwards. This allows readers to see which conclusions rest on the weighing and which remain hypotheses about behaviour.
Finally, an audit should connect its findings to actions that can be checked. If a proposed collection change is introduced, follow-up measurement can ask whether the targeted material actually declines and whether it moves into another stream. A fall in one bin is not automatically a reduction in total waste. The achievement is an evidence-based cycle: define, sample, measure, interpret, act and reassess. Each step makes the next more useful when its assumptions are visible, and each can mislead when a convenient number is treated as the whole story.

reading.title: A harbour makes space for swimming

paragraphs.A: For decades, residents of the fictional port of Esten thought of the inner harbour as a place to work beside rather than enter. Cargo traffic had moved to a larger terminal, but the old quays remained behind fences. When a group proposed an outdoor swimming area, objections concerned more than water quality. Fishing crews still needed access, local businesses feared noise, and some residents doubted that a harbour could feel welcoming. The proposal's supporters began with temporary opening days so that people could experience the site before deciding whether a permanent facility belonged there.
paragraphs.B: Those early days used a floating enclosure close to a disused warehouse. Lifeguards supervised a small number of swimmers, and entry was free. The enclosure kept swimmers separate from boats but did not clean the water. Water testing was therefore essential, and the first opening was cancelled after heavy rainfall. Organisers displayed the cancellation reason at the gate rather than merely posting a notice online. This mattered because some visitors had travelled without checking the website. A disappointing first visit was less damaging to trust when the decision and its evidence were explained clearly.
paragraphs.C: Engineers later traced several drainage routes from streets above the quay. Rain could carry contaminated runoff into the harbour, creating conditions that differed from those measured on dry days. The city improved some drains and introduced a closure protocol based on tests and recent conditions. It did not promise that the swimming area would always be open. Planners considered this uncertainty in the design: a closed pool should not turn the entire waterfront into a dead end. The surrounding deck remained accessible for walking and sitting even when swimming was suspended.
paragraphs.D: Access to the water was another design problem. An ordinary ladder suited confident swimmers but not everyone who wanted to enter. The final enclosure included broad steps and a separate assisted-entry area. Changing cubicles were placed near the entrance, while lockers were visible from the staffed desk. The designers rejected a proposal to locate every service inside the old warehouse because it would force wet swimmers to cross a busy public route. The warehouse instead contained toilets and a classroom used for safety sessions, activities that did not require a direct path from the water.
paragraphs.E: The project also changed who controlled the quay at different times. Fishing crews retained an early-morning unloading period, after which removable barriers opened a wider pedestrian route. A permanent wall would have simplified separation but prevented flexibility. Harbour staff and facility managers met each week during the first summer to resolve problems with delivery times and equipment storage. This routine was less visible than the new deck, yet it made shared use possible. The design depended on agreements that could be adjusted when a fishing boat arrived later than expected or a public event required more space.
paragraphs.F: Counting visitors was straightforward; deciding whom the project served was not. An online survey produced many replies from confident swimmers who had visited repeatedly. Community worker Lena Moss also spoke to older residents at a nearby housing centre and parents at a school. Some liked the waterfront but did not want to swim. Others worried about the cost of lessons rather than admission. Their responses led to a small programme of free introductory sessions. The aim was not to persuade everyone to become a swimmer, but to remove an avoidable barrier for people who wanted to try.
paragraphs.G: By the third summer, the swimming facility had become one attraction among several. A café leased part of the warehouse and helped cover running costs, but its tables occupied only a marked section of the deck. The council wanted to avoid turning a publicly funded waterfront into a place where every seat required a purchase. Free benches remained along the edge, including some outside the busiest view. Maintenance budgets covered replacement of weathered boards and checks of underwater fittings. These recurring expenses were included in public reports alongside attendance, rather than hidden behind the celebration of construction.
paragraphs.H: Esten's fictional harbour was not transformed by a single architectural gesture. Its new use depended on testing, drainage work, access design, operating agreements and attention to people absent from the first survey. Nor did the change erase the port's working identity: fishing activity continued, and swimmers sometimes waited for a delivery to pass. The project suggests that opening a waterfront can mean negotiating a sequence of compatible uses rather than excluding everything that came before. Public access became credible because the city explained its limits and maintained the arrangements that allowed different activities to share a constrained space.

paragraphs.A: An archaeological site does not end at the objects visible on its surface. Buried walls, filled ditches and changes in soil may extend across a much wider area. Excavation can reveal them in detail, but it is slow and changes the deposits it examines. Archaeologists therefore use survey techniques to decide where questions are most promising before opening trenches. In an imagined investigation at North Field, a team compared several ways of reading the ground. None offered an underground photograph. Each measured a physical property from which the team had to infer a possible history.
paragraphs.B: Survey specialist Ada Bell began with aerial images taken after a dry period. Some patches of vegetation had grown differently where buried features altered access to moisture. The marks were useful but inconsistent: a feature visible in one season could disappear in another. Bell compared images from several years and checked whether apparent lines followed modern farm machinery. A striking shape was not automatically ancient. She also recorded blank areas, resisting the temptation to draw a site boundary around only the most attractive marks. Absence in an image might reflect conditions rather than absence in the ground.
paragraphs.C: Geophysicist Ben Ortiz then used an instrument that detected small magnetic variations. In suitable conditions, disturbed soil and some heated materials can differ from surrounding deposits. At North Field, however, recent metal fragments produced strong signals that obscured subtler ones. Ortiz mapped these disturbances rather than simply smoothing them away. The cleaned display was easier to read, but he retained the raw measurements so that later users could see how processing affected interpretation. A visually tidy image can communicate certainty that the underlying observations do not deserve, especially when unexplained noise has been removed.
paragraphs.D: Another team, led by Celine Park, measured electrical resistance along selected lines. Moisture affects how easily current passes through soil, so a buried wall might differ from a filled ditch. Recent rain changed the overall readings, making comparisons between separate days difficult. Park introduced reference measurements in an unchanged strip of ground before each session. These did not solve every problem, but they helped identify variation associated with conditions rather than archaeology. Her results supported one of the magnetic features while leaving another uncertain. The disagreement was treated as a reason for a better question, not a competition to choose one winning instrument.
paragraphs.E: Local historian Dev Rao contributed maps and accounts of land use. A rectangular feature that excited the team as a possible early building appeared at the location of a much later livestock enclosure. The map did not prove the interpretation, because its scale and alignment were imperfect. It nevertheless offered an alternative that had to be considered. Rao also interviewed farmers who remembered changes in drainage. Their recollections were recorded with dates and qualifications rather than treated as either unquestionable truth or mere anecdote. Different evidence carried different uncertainties, and comparison required preserving those distinctions.
paragraphs.F: The team eventually opened two small trenches. One confirmed a stone foundation, while the other exposed a modern drain where a promising linear signal had appeared. This mixed result was more useful than a simple success story. It showed that the survey had located real differences in the ground without always identifying their cause correctly. The trench records were linked to the survey archive, including the unsuccessful interpretation. Future researchers would therefore be able to revisit the decision process instead of seeing only the feature that justified the team's original enthusiasm.
paragraphs.G: There was also a question of where not to dig. A patch containing fragile deposits was left untouched because the immediate research question could be answered elsewhere. Non-invasive survey did not make excavation unnecessary; it helped target an irreversible action. The landowner wanted assurance that the whole field would not be opened, and a public explanation described the planned limits. Protecting archaeological information involved preserving some uncertainty. A feature could remain an informed possibility until a future project had a compelling reason and a suitable method to investigate it more directly.
paragraphs.H: North Field's fictional investigation illustrates the difference between detecting a pattern and explaining it. Instruments extend perception, but their outputs become evidence through decisions about conditions, processing and comparison. A survey image can look authoritative while concealing several plausible interpretations. Good reporting makes that uncertainty usable rather than merely adding a vague warning at the end. The result is a map of questions as well as features: where evidence agrees, where it conflicts, and where a future observer might learn something new without repeating damage that has already been done.

paragraphs.A: When an institution uses a model to rank applications, explanation can appear to be an optional courtesy added after the result. A person receives a decision and perhaps a sentence describing the system's general purpose. Yet decisions allocate opportunities, and an explanation may be necessary for identifying an error or challenging an inappropriate rule. The question is not simply whether the model can produce a plausible account of its operation. It is whether the institution gives the affected person information that serves a practical purpose, together with a route for acting on it.
paragraphs.B: Different audiences require different explanations. An engineer investigating a calculation may need a detailed account of data transformations. An applicant may need to know that an outdated address caused the system to assign the wrong eligibility category. Providing the engineer's report to the applicant can satisfy a formal requirement while failing to help. Technical completeness and practical intelligibility are not identical. An institution should begin by asking what the recipient must be able to understand or do, rather than assuming that more mathematical detail always makes a decision more accountable.
paragraphs.C: Consider a fictional scholarship programme. Its ranking model awards additional weight to applicants from areas with limited educational resources. An applicant who recently moved is assigned to a better-resourced area using an old record. Explaining that neighbourhood data influenced the score is useful, but incomplete. The applicant needs to know which address was used and how to correct it. More importantly, the programme needs a procedure for reviewing the decision after correction. Information without a responsive process may merely describe an injustice accurately while leaving its consequence unchanged.
paragraphs.D: Explanation also has limits when the rule itself is disputed. A perfectly accurate account of a policy does not make the policy fair. People may agree on how a model treated distance from a training centre while disagreeing on whether distance should count at all. This disagreement cannot be resolved by showing that the software performed its calculation correctly. It requires institutional reasons and, where appropriate, public debate. Technical auditing remains valuable, but it answers a narrower question than the legitimacy of the objective that the institution has instructed the system to pursue.
paragraphs.E: Some critics argue that explanations will enable people to manipulate a system. The concern is real when a disclosed threshold allows someone to alter a superficial signal without meeting the policy's purpose. Nevertheless, secrecy can also shield errors and arbitrary rules. Institutions need to distinguish exploitable operational details from information necessary for a meaningful challenge. An applicant should not have to accept a demonstrably false record merely because the ranking method is commercially sensitive. The burden of finding an appropriate form of disclosure belongs primarily to the institution using the system, not to the person affected by it.
paragraphs.F: Nor is an appealing explanation necessarily faithful. A model can generate a simple story that sounds reasonable without identifying what actually determined its output. If staff repeat such stories without checking them, explanation becomes a technique for discouraging questions. A useful account should be tested against the decision process and should state where certainty is limited. In some cases the honest answer is that a particular contribution cannot be isolated reliably. That admission may be less satisfying than a confident narrative, but it gives a reviewer a more accurate basis for deciding whether further investigation is needed.
paragraphs.G: Human review is often offered as a remedy, although the phrase can conceal very different arrangements. A reviewer with no time, authority or additional information may simply confirm the original result. Meaningful review requires the ability to change it and a reasoned record of the judgement. It also requires attention to recurring patterns: correcting one applicant's address should lead the programme to ask whether similar errors affect others. Otherwise an appeal system can become a costly way of repairing individual cases while leaving a predictable source of harm operating unchanged.
paragraphs.H: Accountability therefore belongs to an institution, even when a complex model makes part of its work difficult to describe. A supplier may assist with analysis, but cannot absorb the public body's responsibility to justify the service it provides. Good explanations connect facts, rules and remedies in language suited to the recipient. Their value lies not in making every refusal pleasant or every dispute disappear, but in making mistakes contestable and policy choices visible. A decision becomes more accountable when the person receiving it can do more than admire the sophistication of the machinery behind it.

writing.prompt: The diagram shows a proposed industrial process for turning used cork stoppers into floor panels. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
writing.visual:
![Cork panel process](writing-1.svg)

Accessible diagram transcription:

1. Collect used cork stoppers.
2. Sort: reject non-cork items (leave the process).
3. Wash accepted cork.
4. Dry with warm air.
5. Grind into granules.
6. Mix granules with a supplied binder.
7. Press the mixture into panels using heat and pressure.
8. Inspect panels: suitable panels go to packing and sale; unsuitable panels are ground again and returned to the mixing stage.

The binder enters only at mixing. The diagram supplies no times, temperatures or quantities.
writing.guidance: Give an overview of collection, preparation, manufacture and inspection, including the feedback loop. Distinguish rejected non-cork input leaving the process from failed cork panels returning to grinding/mixing. Mention binder input and heat/pressure without inventing numerical conditions. This is an authored proposed process, not a claim about every cork factory.

writing.prompt: More employers are offering flexible working hours. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons and relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
writing.guidance: Evaluate flexible hours, rather than discussing only home working. Explain benefits and costs for workers or organisations and make a clear comparative judgement. Coordination, service coverage and caring responsibilities are relevant examples. A claim that there are advantages and disadvantages without weighing them leaves the main question unanswered.
